Course index and how to use this material
Who this is for
Someone who has never studied trees. You should be comfortable with C++ basics: functions,
pointers at a beginner level, vector, queue, stack, and simple recursion such as factorial. Nothing
else is assumed. Recursion is reintroduced from scratch in Part 1 where it is needed.
What you will be able to do at the end
Open any LeetCode Easy tree problem and solve it in ten minutes. Open a typical Medium tree
problem and know within a minute which of five patterns it belongs to, then implement it. More
importantly , look at a problem you have never seen and ask the right questions:
What information does each subtree need to return?
Is this DFS, BFS, or bottom-up?
What should my base case be?
What do I combine from the left and the right?
Memorising twenty solutions is not the goal, and does not work. Recognising five patterns does.

Part 1: Tree Fundamentals
Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures
Why trees exist
Arrays, vectors and linked lists all store data in a straight line. That works when the data itself is a
line: marks of 50 students, characters of a string, prices over 30 days.
A lot of real data is not a line. It is a hierarchy .
Company
|-- Engineering
| |-- Backend
| +-- Frontend
+-- Sales
|-- India
+-- Europe
Folders inside folders, an HTML page inside body inside html, a tournament bracket, a family lineage,
the decision steps of a game. In all of these, one item leads to several items below it, and each of
those again leads to more. You cannot express that with a single line of memory without a lot of pain.
There is a second reason, a purely practical one. A sorted array searches in O(log N) but inserting in
the middle costs O(N). A linked list inserts in O(1) but searches in O(N). A balanced search tree gives

the middle costs O(N). A linked list inserts in O(1) but searches in O(N). A balanced search tree gives
you both search and insert in O(log N). Databases, file systems, std::map and std::set are all built
on trees for exactly this reason.
So trees exist for two reasons:
1. Some data is naturally hierarchical.
2. Some operations are only fast when data is arranged in a branching structure.
For this course we care mostly about the first reason, because that is what LeetCode tree problems
test.
What is a tree
A tree is a set of nodes connected by edges, with three rules:
1. One node is marked special. It is called the root, and it is drawn at the top.
2. Every other node has exactly one node directly above it (its parent).
1

3. There are no cycles. You can never walk down and come back to where you started.
Because of rule 2 and 3, a tree with N nodes always has exactly N - 1 edges. Every node except the
root consumes exactly one edge to attach itself to its parent.
Computer science trees are drawn upside down. Root on top, leaves at the bottom. Get used to it now,
every diagram in this material follows that convention.

Level: nodes at the same distance from the root form a level. Level 0 = {1}, level 1 = {2, 3}, level 2
= {4, 5, 6}.
Depth of a node: number of edges from the root down to that node. Depth(1) = 0, depth(2) = 1,
depth(4) = 2. Depth is measured looking upward, toward the root.
Height of a node: number of edges on the longest path from that node down to a leaf. Height(4) =
0, height(2) = 1, height(1) = 2. Height is measured looking downward.
Height of the tree: the height of its root. Here, 2.
Depth versus height, and the counting trap
Depth and height are measured in opposite directions. A leaf has height 0. The root has depth 0.
There is a second trap. Some books count edges, some count nodes. A single node alone has height 0
by the edge definition and height 1 by the node definition. Both are used in the real world.
LeetCode uses the node count. Problem 104, “Maximum Depth of Binary Tree”, says the depth of the
tree above is 3, not 2.

Rule for this course:
• When we write a LeetCode style function calledmaxDepth or height, we count nodes, so an empty
tree returns 0 and a single node returns 1.
• When we discuss theory such as “the height of a perfect tree is log N”, we count edges.
Whenever you sit down to code, decide which one you are using in the first ten seconds, and make
the base case agree with it. Almost every off-by-one bug in tree code comes from skipping this step.
Binary tree
A binary tree is a tree where every node has at most two children, and the two children are
distinguishable: one is the left child, one is the right child.

Why the shape matters
Two numbers you should be able to state instantly:
• A perfect tree of height h has 2ˆ(h+1) - 1 nodes. Level d holds at most 2ˆd nodes.
• Therefore a balanced tree with N nodes has height about log2(N). For N = 10ˆ6 that is about 20.
A skewed tree with N nodes has height N - 1.

Every recursive tree algorithm uses O(H) stack space, where H is the height. On a balanced tree that
is 20 stack frames. On a skewed tree of 10ˆ5 nodes that is 10ˆ5 stack frames, and on some judges
that is a stack overflow. When you see “the tree can be skewed” in constraints, that is the hint.

A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree with one extra promise:

TreeNode *right;
TreeNode(int x) : val(x), left(NULL), right(NULL) {}
};

The array representation
A complete binary tree can be stored in a plain array with no pointers at all:
• node at index i has children at 2*i + 1 and 2*i + 2
• its parent is at (i - 1) / 2
index: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6
value: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
This is how heaps and segment trees are built. For general binary trees it wastes memory (a skewed
tree of 20 nodes would need an array of size 2ˆ20), so LeetCode problems use pointers.

You will see input like:

That is level order, left to right, with null marking a missing child. Read it as:

level 1: 2 3

Why recursion fits trees so naturally
A quick recursion refresher
A recursive function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It needs two parts:
1. a base case, small enough to answer directly
2. a recursive step, which solves a smaller input and builds the answer from it

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 7
int fact(int n) {
if (n == 0) return 1; // base case
return n * fact(n - 1); // smaller version of the same problem
}
When you call fact(3), the machine does not magically know the answer. It stacks up pending work:
fact(3) waits for fact(2)
fact(2) waits for fact(1)
fact(1) waits for fact(0)
fact(0) = 1 <- base case, now unwind
fact(1) = 1 * 1 = 1
fact(2) = 2 * 1 = 2
fact(3) = 3 * 2 = 6
Two things to notice, because they reappear in every tree problem:
• The going-down phase and the coming-back-up phase are different moments. You can do work in
either one.
• Every pending call sits on the call stack, which costs memory .
Now the tree version
For an array you had to invent the smaller problem: n - 1 , or “the rest of the array”. In a tree the
smaller problem is already sitting there. root->left is a smaller tree. root->right is a smaller tree.

Learn to draw this diagram. When a recursive tree solution misbehaves, drawing the call tree for a 5

Common mistakes
• Forgetting the NULL base case. Then root->val dereferences a null pointer and you get a
runtime error or a segfault. Write the if (root == NULL) line first, before anything else.
• Checking the child instead of the node. Writing if (root->left == NULL) return ... at the
top means an empty tree still crashes, and the logic gets duplicated for both sides. Guard the node
itself.

• Checking the child instead of the node. Writing if (root->left == NULL) return ... at the
top means an empty tree still crashes, and the logic gets duplicated for both sides. Guard the node
itself.
• Mixing up height and depth. Depth counts downward from the root, height counts upward from
the leaves.
• Mixing up edge counting and node counting. Decide first, then write the base case to match.
• Assuming a plain binary tree is a BST. Only assume ordering when the problem says so.
• Assuming a leaf means “one child is NULL”. A leaf means both children are NULL. This one
specific mistake breaks the Minimum Depth problem for almost everyone the first time.
• Forgetting that the tree can be a single long chain. Recursion depth equals height, not log N.

Part 2: Depth First Traversals
Preorder, Inorder, Postorder
What traversal means
Traversal means visiting every node exactly once in some fixed order. That is all.
An array has one obvious order: left to right. A tree does not. From node 1 you can go to 2 or to 3,
and there is no single natural answer. Different orders are useful for different jobs, so we standardise
a few of them and give them names.
Depth First Search (DFS) means: go as deep as possible down one branch before coming back and
trying the other branch. It is what a person does in a maze when they follow one corridor to its end
before backtracking.
Breadth First Search (BFS) means: finish an entire level before moving to the next. That is Part 3.
DFS on a binary tree comes in three flavours. They differ in exactly one thing: when you record the
current node relative to the two recursive calls.
// preorder
visit(node); go(left); go(right);
// inorder
go(left); visit(node); go(right);
// postorder

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 2
During that walk you touch every node exactly three times:
1. when you arrive at it from above (going down into it)
2. when you come back up from its left subtree
3. when you come back up from its right subtree, just before leaving it for good
Now the three traversals are simply three choices of which touch counts:
Traversal Record the node on which touch
Preorder 1st touch, on the way down
Inorder 2nd touch, between left and right
Postorder 3rd touch, on the way out
The results for our tree:
Preorder : 1 2 4 5 3 6
Inorder : 4 2 5 1 3 6
Postorder : 4 5 2 6 3 1
Check those three lines against the picture until they feel obvious. Once this single picture is solid,
iterative traversal and Morris traversal later become much less mysterious, because they are just
different ways of remembering “which touch am I on”.
Preorder traversal
Meaning
Process the node, then everything on its left, then everything on its right. Root comes before its

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 3
vector<int> preorderTraversal(TreeNode* root) {
vector<int> out;
preorder(root, out);
return out;
}
Note the vector<int>&. The ampersand means all calls share one vector. Drop it and every call gets
its own copy , the pushes are thrown away , and you return an empty answer. This is one of the most
common beginner bugs in tree code.

call preorder(2) record 2 out = [1,2]

|-- pre(2)

+-- pre(6)

Complexity
Time O(N): every node is entered once and does O(1) work. Space O(H) for the call stack, where H is
the height. O(log N) if balanced, O(N) if skewed. The output vector is a separate O(N), which we
usually do not count as extra space since it is the answer.
When preorder is the right choice
• Copying or cloning a tree. You must create the parent before you can attach children to it.
• Serialising a tree so it can be rebuilt later. Preorder plus null markers is enough to reconstruct a
tree uniquely .
• Building a tree from preorder plus inorder arrays (LeetCode 105). The first element of preorder

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 4
is always the root.
• Passing information downward, for example “here is the path from the root to you” or “here is
the sum so far”. Anything the parent knows and the child needs is naturally handed over on the
way down. This is the shape of all root-to-leaf path problems in Part 9.
The rule of thumb: preorder is the traversal for top-down information flow.
Common mistakes
• Forgetting & on the output vector.
• Putting the push_back after the two calls “because it looks tidier”. That is postorder, and the
output changes.
• Checking if (root->left != NULL) preorder(root->left) instead of guarding inside the
function. It works, but it doubles the number of conditions you must get right, and it breaks
immediately for an empty tree.

When inorder is the right choice
• Anything involving a BST. The inorder traversal of a BST is sorted, ascending. This single fact
solves a whole family of problems: validate BST (LeetCode 98), kth smallest element (230),
minimum absolute difference (530), convert BST to sorted list, and more.
• Finding the predecessor or successor of a node in a BST.
• Recovering a tree when you are given the inorder array plus preorder or postorder.

Why is a BST’s inorder sorted? By definition, everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node
and everything in the right subtree is larger. Inorder prints exactly in that order: smaller stuff, node,
larger stuff. Apply the same reasoning inside each subtree and the whole sequence is sorted.
Common mistakes
• Assuming inorder is sorted for a general binary tree. It is not. On our tree it is 4 2 5 1 3 6, which
is nowhere near sorted. That property is a BST property , not a tree property .
• In “validate BST”, checking only left->val < root->val < right->val . That is a local check
and it is wrong. Either do an inorder walk and confirm it is strictly increasing, or pass a valid (min,
max) range downward.
• Losing the previous value while validating. You need to remember the previously printed node to

max) range downward.

Postorder traversal

Binary Trees and Tree Data Structures 6
Meaning
Everything on the left, everything on the right, and only then the node itself. The root is always last.
Recursive algorithm

if node is empty: return
postorder(node.left)
postorder(node.right)
